title: KV cache eviction & paging deep dive with Orion Tech
summary: Technical deep dive on KV cache eviction, paging, long-context handling, and prefix reuse issues observed in Orion's prod workload. Discussed root causes — high prefix churn, small per-shard cache sizes, and paging / GPU memory compaction — plus mitigations: tuned eviction policies, per-prefix TTLs, smarter prefix hashing, and config changes for batching and quantization. Agreed next steps to run benchmarks and share config/playbook.
next_steps: Alex Chen: Share KV-cache design doc + perf spreadsheet (due: 2026-06-12)
Samir Patel: Run targeted eviction benchmark on Orion sample traces (due: 2026-06-17)
Priya Kapoor / Orion: Provide representative 10k user session traces (due: 2026-06-15)
Schedule follow-up deep dive to review benchmark results (tentative: 2026-06-24)

Samir Patel: run eviction/paging benchmark and share logs (due: 2026-06-17)

transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we're a little over the hour. My name's Alex Chen, AE on Redwood Inference, with me Samir (SE) and Rosa from CS. Can you all hear us?
[00:12] Priya Kapoor: Yeah loud and clear. Thanks Alex. Michael and Jules are here too.
[00:18] Michael Rivera (CTO): Hi all. We're hoping to get to the bottom of a pattern where KV cache evictions spike and tail latencies go up.
[00:30] Alex Chen (AE): Great. Samir, do you want to frame the agenda?
[00:33] Samir Patel (SE): Sure. We'll first review Orion's symptom timeline, dig into KV cache size/eviction metrics, look at paging events and GPU mem compaction, then discuss mitigations — eviction policy, per-prefix TTLs, prefix hashing, batching and quantization tradeoffs, and private/VPC constraints.
[00:48] Jules Park (Infra): Quick note — we saw eviction bursts coincident with marketing surges and long multi-step chat sessions. Our cache hit rate drops from 92% to 60% in ~10 minutes.
[01:02] Samir Patel (SE): That matches a churn pattern; so two hypotheses: small per-shard cache capacity relative to working set, or high prefix diversity causing low reuse.
[01:12] Priya Kapoor: Our team definitely has high prefix churn — many unique session prompts with small variations. We also use user-specific prefixes for personalization.
[01:20] Alex Chen (AE): Ok, let's pull some metrics. Jules, can you share the shard sizing?
[01:25] Jules Park: We're on 8xA100-80GB per cluster pool. Each model server shard has ~6GB reserved for KV cache after other allocations.
[01:34] Samir Patel (SE): 6GB per shard can be tight for long-context + personalization if your tokens per session often go beyond 2.5k. With large prefix diversity, LRU can evict useful entries quickly.
[01:46] Priya Kapoor: We did enable LRU default. Is there a better algorithm?
[01:50] Samir Patel (SE): We recommend a reuse-aware policy — not just plain LRU. Options: segmented LRU (long-term vs short-term), LFU hybrid, or TTL per prefix based on reuse score. Also consider adaptive per-prefix sizing when you detect hot prefixes.
[02:05] Michael Rivera: How invasive are those changes? We can't change tokenization schema overnight.
[02:10] Alex Chen (AE): Most changes are config-first. Seg-LRU or LFU can be enabled as a runtime config; TTL tagging requires a small app-side header to mark session types but doesn't need model changes.
[02:20] Priya Kapoor: We rely on user-id prefixes to personalize, which multiplies prefix count. Would hashing prefixes to a smaller namespace help?
[02:28] Samir Patel (SE): Yes, prefix canonicalization and bucketed hashing can increase reuse. BUT be careful — naive hashing can cause false sharing across unrelated sessions. We use namespace-aware hashing e.g. user-id -> bucket range plus intent hash.
[02:43] Alex Chen (AE): Also consider prefix fingerprinting to collapse near-duplicates — small diffs in system messages often break reuse.
[02:50] Jules Park: We also saw GPU paging/compaction events reported by the runtime during eviction spikes. Explain that?
[02:57] Samir Patel (SE): Paging often happens when the runtime evicts large KV frames and the GPU driver triggers memory compaction, or if model activations plus KV exceed the soft limit. Frequent small allocations + deallocations increase fragmentation, leading to OOM-ish behaviour and CPU<->GPU stalls.
[03:14] Priya Kapoor: Is this more likely on 80GB A100 than on smaller cards?
[03:18] Samir Patel (SE): Actually fragmentation is independent of total size; it's about allocation pattern. But smaller per-shard reserves reduce headroom for bursty multi-session contexts.
[03:27] Alex Chen (AE): Can we instrument the compaction events? Jules, are you collecting nvidia-smi and runtime logs?
[03:33] Jules Park: Yes, we have driver logs. We can share.
[03:36] Samir Patel (SE): Please include CUDA memory events and runtime eviction traces. We'll correlate timestamps — compaction events should line up with eviction spikes.
[03:44] Michael Rivera: On quantization — we use 8-bit for model weights to save memory. Any conflicts with KV cache?
[03:50] Samir Patel (SE): Quantization reduces model memory but increases per-token compute in some kernels; it doesn't directly increase KV cache size. However, if quantization changes runtime kernel choices, hot-path memory layout can move and change allocation fragmentation. Also some quantized kernels pin memory differently which affects when compaction triggers.
[04:07] Priya Kapoor: So quantization might indirectly influence eviction/paging. Interesting.
[04:11] Alex Chen (AE): Another axis is batching. You're running low-latency config?
[04:15] Jules Park: We set target p99 latency 400ms and micro-batch size 1 for foreground traffic, with background batchers for throughput.
[04:24] Samir Patel (SE): Continuous batching helps throughput but can increase peak memory using KV while waiting for batch. If your long-context requests are batched, they hold KV entries longer, increasing working set. Consider priority-aware batching where long-context / personalized sessions are favored for immediate dispatch to avoid holding KV across batches.
[04:43] Priya Kapoor: We could mark session type on the request to guide the router/dispatcher. Any config examples?
[04:48] Samir Patel (SE): We'll share sample router config where requests set header X-Session-Type: long-context | short, and runtime uses that to pick a lane with different batching windows.
[04:58] Alex Chen (AE): Let's talk prefix reuse pitfalls. We saw false negatives due to tokenization differences right?
[05:03] Priya Kapoor: Yes — small punctuation changes create different token sequences so the KV key doesn't match.
[05:10] Samir Patel (SE): Two approaches: 1) canonicalize prompts before hashing (strip punctuation, normalize whitespace for system messages), and 2) use fuzzy prefix matching (k-nearest prefix lookup) with a compact signature like simhash across normalized tokens. Tradeoff is compute overhead vs hit rate.
[05:27] Michael Rivera: Fuzzy lookup sounds heavy. Wouldn't that add latency?
[05:31] Samir Patel (SE): Done on the router side it's cheap — we only compute signatures on session start and compare against active hot-key table. It's an O(1) or small-k lookup with bloom filters to reduce false scanning. Latency impact is minimal if implemented in C++ or Rust path.
[05:44] Alex Chen (AE): There's also the idea of prefix TTL: short-lived personalization prefixes get small TTLs, global system messages get long TTLs. That reduces cache churn.
[05:53] Priya Kapoor: How do we set TTLs automatically? Heuristics? ML?
[05:58] Samir Patel (SE): Start with heuristics based on prefix cardinality and reuse: high-cardinality prefixes (user-id) -> short TTL; low-cardinality -> long TTL. We can later use an ML model to predict reuse score.
[06:10] Jules Park: You mentioned adaptive per-prefix sizing — how heavy is that to run?
[06:14] Samir Patel (SE): It's a runtime sampling loop: track per-prefix hit counters and allocate soft quotas. It's a few percent CPU overhead and needs small metadata storage. We provide it as an optional module; turning it on is a config flag.
[06:25] Priya Kapoor: Ok good. Now about paging — what immediate mitigations?
[06:29] Samir Patel (SE): Short-term: increase soft KV reserve by 20% if cluster headroom allows; enable slab allocation tuning to reduce fragmentation; compact less aggressively by adjusting driver GC tuning; move very long KV frames to a paged region backed by host RAM with async fetch (tradeoff latency).
[06:48] Michael Rivera: That last option worries us — pulling KV from host RAM will increase tail latency.
[06:52] Alex Chen (AE): Right — we only recommend host-backed paging for background workloads or infrequent cold prefixes. For foreground low-latency traffic it's a last resort.
[07:02] Priya Kapoor: Any telemetry we should add to detect early signs?
[07:06] Samir Patel (SE): Watch increasing allocation/deallocation rate, rising fragmentation metric (our runtime exposes 'gpu_mem_frag_pct'), sudden drop in reuse ratio, and a correlation between small batch size increases and eviction spikes. We'll share a Grafana dashboard template.
[07:22] Jules Park: On private/VPC deployment: we're evaluating Redwood Private but need assurances on KMS/HSM integration and audit logs. Will that impact KV cache behaviour?
[07:31] Alex Chen (AE): No functional impact on KV cache. Private deployment affects how we wire KMS and networking. We can run the same runtime; audit logs and KMS only change control plane and key storage. Nonethless, on-prem VMs may have different PCIe topologies which can influence GPU memory behavior; we'll need to benchmark on your target hardware.
[07:50] Priya Kapoor: Good point. We'll share hardware details.
[07:53] Michael Rivera: About replication and fallback — can Redwood route to smaller quantized variants if a shard is overloaded?
[07:59] Samir Patel (SE): Yes, smart routing can fallback to a quantized or smaller-context model to preserve availability. That reduces KV reliance for that request class. You can define policies: latency-first vs cost-first.
[08:12] Alex Chen (AE): Ok, let's look at a real trace. Jules, can you paste the eviction timeline?
[08:17] Jules Park: (shares screen) Here's a 30-minute window: 14:12 to 14:42. At 14:15 we see a spike in unique prefixes, eviction rate jumps, then GPU compaction events at 14:16:02 and 14:16:09, p99 latency increases.
[08:34] Samir Patel (SE): That pattern suggests a burst of new sessions with long context. If the runtime had prepopulated hot prefix entries, it wouldn't have evicted. But churn replaced hot entries rapidly.
[08:45] Priya Kapoor: The burst was from a marketing email — lots of users hitting onboarding flows with extra system prompts.
[08:51] Alex Chen (AE): Practical mitigation: treat marketing traffic as a separate lane with higher per-shard KV allocation or route it to a different cluster sized for churn.
[09:00] Priya Kapoor: We could route based on source header.
[09:04] Samir Patel (SE): Exactly. Also pre-warming: if you can predict the burst window, pre-warm cache with likely onboarding prefixes. We'll share a pre-warm playbook.
[09:14] Jules Park: One puzzling thing is prefix reuse within a session — sometimes we don't reuse earlier KV entries even though user continues same thread. Any pointers?
[09:22] Samir Patel (SE): Often it's due to prompt drift: small system message modifications later in the session that change token offsets — KV keys include position id and prefix fingerprint, so drift breaks the match. Use positional-agnostic keys for portions of the prompt, or store multi-granularity keys: short n-gram prefixes plus full prefixes.
[09:39] Priya Kapoor: Multi-granularity sounds promising but increases metadata.
[09:43] Samir Patel (SE): Yes, it's a space vs hit-rate tradeoff. We recommend storing short-fingerprint entries for all sessions (cheap) and long-full entries only for hot prefixes.
[09:55] Michael Rivera: Any quick wins we can implement in the next week?
[09:58] Alex Chen (AE): Yes: 1) enable segmented LRU, 2) add X-Session-Type header and route marketing bursts to a separate lane, 3) increase per-shard KV soft reserve by 15% if possible, 4) export traces and driver logs and send to Samir. These are minimal-risk.
[10:15] Priya Kapoor: We'll do that.
[10:18] Samir Patel (SE): Now a note on prefix hashing collisions — if you bucket too coarsely you'll get false-positive reuse which returns spurious KV leading to bad outputs. We always include a nonce/checksum in the stored value so on lookup we validate content; if mismatch we fallback and optionally promote correct prefix.
[10:36] Alex Chen (AE): Good point. That protects quality. Also watch out for same-prefix reuse across different intents — you might need intent tags.
[10:44] Priya Kapoor: About telemetry — we'll add the dashboard and the 'gpu_mem_frag_pct' metric. Anything else?
[10:50] Samir Patel (SE): 'kv_hit_rate_by_prefix_class', 'eviction_rate', 'alloc_dealloc_rate', and 'background_paging_count' are key. We'll provide the Grafana JSON.
[11:01] Jules Park: On quantization profiles — we're on per-layer 8-bit with some layers in 16-bit. We saw slightly higher CPU pre/post processing.
[11:09] Samir Patel (SE): That's expected. Also if you use 4-bit Aggressive quantization to save memory you might see different kernel selection and temporarily more fragmentation; test it under trace.
[11:22] Priya Kapoor: We can try a canary with 4-bit on a subset.
[11:26] Samir Patel (SE): Good. Make sure you run the end-to-end trace with same prompt set. We'll help configure canary.
[11:33] Alex Chen (AE): Let's capture concrete timeline for follow-up: Samir will run eviction benchmark, Alex will share docs, Jules will share traces and hardware details, Priya will coordinate.
[11:45] Priya Kapoor: Quick question — do you have a recommended eviction threshold for user-id prefixes vs system prompts?
[11:51] Samir Patel (SE): Start with TTL 5 minutes for user-id prefixes, 30+ minutes for system prompts, and tune from there. If you have very long-lived sessions, increase user TTL but cap per-user stored frames to a small N (e.g., last 3 frames).
[12:07] Michael Rivera: For the paged region idea, what typical tail latency penalty do you see?
[12:12] Samir Patel (SE): Host-backed paging adds median +30-80ms when cold, but if you have async prefetch and good locality it can be <20ms for warm hits. Depends on interconnect (PCIe Gen4 vs NVLink).
[12:26] Jules Park: We're on NVLink within node but PCIe to host is Gen4. We'll include topology.
[12:32] Alex Chen (AE): We'll also propose a routing fallback: if KV miss and model time > X we fallback to small quantized variant to serve sooner.
[12:41] Priya Kapoor: Sounds good. Any security concerns with KV content in Private?
[12:45] Alex Chen (AE): For Private deployments you control disk and RAM encryption; runtime can integrate with KMS to encrypt stored KV frames at rest. Audit logs capture access. We'll include recommended KMS integration steps.
[12:57] Samir Patel (SE): One more implementation detail: coalesced eviction vs single-frame eviction. Coalesced eviction evicts groups to reduce fragmentation but can lead to larger miss windows; single-frame evict is more targeted but costs more cycles. We usually default to coalesced during low-load and single-frame during spikes.
[13:16] Priya Kapoor: Do you have any scripts to replay traces for the benchmark?
[13:20] Samir Patel (SE): Yes, we'll share a replay harness that simulates sessions with original timing and prefixes. It can run locally or in your staging.
[13:28] Michael Rivera: Excellent.
[13:31] Alex Chen (AE): We should record the main decisions.
[13:34] (15 min of detailed instrumentation discussion and log parsing omitted for brevity; attendees reviewed heap/kv histograms and bucket distributions)
[28:40] Samir Patel (SE): Back to next steps — I'll run two benchmarks: 1) baseline with current config, 2) tuned with segmented LRU + per-prefix TTL and route marketing traffic off main lane.
[28:53] Jules Park: We'll provide traces and hardware/topology by tomorrow.
[28:57] Priya Kapoor: We'll also try a short canary with a small 4-bit quantized model on 1 shard.
[29:04] Alex Chen (AE): Great. Any final questions?
[29:07] Michael Rivera: One last — what's the best way to validate that prefix canonicalization didn't affect quality?
[29:12] Samir Patel (SE): Run an A/B on a small percent: canonicalized prompts vs control, measure hallucination/regression metrics and LLM evals. We'll help set up the eval harness.
[29:24] Priya Kapoor: Perfect.
[29:26] Alex Chen (AE): Ok, recap and owners: Alex send docs, Samir run benchmarks, Jules provide traces/hardware, Priya coordinate canary and session traces, Rosa share VPC/KMS checklist. We'll reconvene after Samir's benchmark results.
[29:40] Jules Park: Thanks everyone.
[29:43] Michael Rivera: Thanks.
[29:45] (call ends)

Notes: transcript has been lightly cleaned for legibility; some speaker attributions may be approximate. Attachments referenced: KV cache design doc (link to be emailed), Grafana dashboard JSON, eviction benchmark harness.
